articles.title: Denis Leary says firefighters’ darkest days after 9/11 helped bring hit show ‘Rescue Me’ to life
articles.summary: Denis Leary watched FDNY firefighters shift from crushing grief to laughter in minutes, a raw moment that shaped "Rescue Me" into a landmark drama.
articles.body: Denis Leary saw grief and laughter collide inside FDNY firehouses in the devastating aftermath of 9/11 – an emotional whiplash that ultimately helped inspire "Rescue Me." That collision of heartbreak and humor would become central to "Rescue Me," with Leary drawing from the firefighters he knew and the raw moments he witnessed inside their firehouses in the months after 9/11. "A lot of the guys I knew that had survived, I was spending time with them and in their firehouses as they were digging through The Pile in the fall right after 9/11," he told the New York Post. "We were witnessing the grief that they were going through." TWENTY-FIVE YEARS LATER, HOLLYWOOD IS GIVING 9/11 THE SILENT TREATMENT, AND IT’S MAKING US LESS SAFE The original idea Leary was working on with writer Peter Tolan was about a firefighter killed in the line of duty, but one moment changed his mind completely. "It was literally in the blink of an eye," he explained. "We went from watching a guy come up from downtown from The Pile – they had found a friend, a piece of a friend, and so he was just overwhelmed with grief. I mean, he could barely talk." "Watching him trying to fight to talk in that firehouse kitchen was a very tough experience to watch," Leary recalled. "Maybe 20 minutes later…all of us were laughing about something." That moment – moving from crushing grief to laughter in a matter of minutes – helped Leary envision what "Rescue Me" could become. MICHAEL KEATON SAYS 9/11 FILM ‘WORTH’ IS ABOUT EMPATHY "We’re going to make a show where people are on the edge of their seat watching an action sequence involving fire," Leary told the outlet. "And then the next minute they’re crying because they’re so sad, and then the minute after that, they’re laughing their a---s off." "Rescue Me" stars Leary as Tommy Gavin, a veteran New York City firefighter struggling with alcoholism, family turmoil and survivor’s guilt in the aftermath of the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks. The supporting cast includes Andrea Roth, Michael Lombardi, Steven Pasquale, Daniel Sunjata, John Scurti and Jack McGee. Leary and Tolan didn't have to hunt for information. FDNY members and firefighting consultants gave the show's creators plenty of real-life firehouse stories to draw from. Watching him trying to fight to talk in that firehouse kitchen was a very tough experience to watch. Maybe 20 minutes later…all of us were laughing about something." "We had so much information on a daily basis, not just comedically, I’m talking about dramatically," Leary said. "All the ideas for our fires came basically from experiences those guys had." Feedback from younger firefighters was overwhelmingly positive before the show's launch, according to Leary. "They said, ‘You got it. You totally nailed it.'" He watched an "endless flow" of dust-covered corporate workers fleeing uptown New York City for hours from the West Side Highway. "They turned the rink into a morgue, and they lined up all the ambulances," he recalled. Leary added, "The sound of the buildings … it’s almost like it goes into your bones." Leary had experienced the bond between firefighters firsthand years earlier, after his cousin and close friend Jeremiah Lucey was killed alongside five other Worcester firefighters in a 1999 warehouse fire. He recalled FDNY friends traveling to Massachusetts to help search the ruins. The actor launched the Leary Firefighters Foundation in 2000, shortly before the 9/11 attacks took the lives of many FDNY firefighters and friends of Leary. "I knew I was going to hear about firefighter friends of mine from the FDNY that didn’t make it," Leary recalled. "But the next day, to hear that 'Ace' Bailey had died in the thing as well, we were just like, ‘That is crazy.’ I mean, it’s insanity." Reflecting on the series alongside Leary at the 9/11 Memorial & Museum in 2024, Tolan – co-creator of the show – acknowledged the weight of building a television series around a tragedy that remained deeply personal for so many. "When you know that, you always have to sort of be vigilant to how far am I going and is it too soon to do this? And I'm not going to say that we were hugely careful because there are elements of the show that are raucous – that are just inappropriately funny," Tolan said. "But that's the human experience." articles.title: Kailash Kher sells 2,619 sq ft office space in Mumbai's BKC for Rs 10..75 crore, earns profit of Rs 25 lakh: Report
articles.summary: Singer Kailash Kher has sold a commercial office space in Mumbai’s Bandra Kurla Complex (BKC) for Rs 10.75 crore, less than a year after purchasing it.
articles.body: Singer Kailash Kher has sold a commercial office space in Mumbai’s Bandra Kurla Complex (BKC) for Rs 10.75 crore, less than a year after purchasing it for Rs 10.50 crore. According to property registration details accessed by CRE Matrix, the transaction has fetched Kher Rs 25 lakh more than what he paid for the property.The sale was registered on September 9, 2026, with Lakewater Retail Private Limited as the buyer.The office is located on the seventh floor of Trade Centre, opposite the MTNL Building in BKC, Bandra East. Spread across a carpet area of 2,619 sq ft, the commercial unit also comes with one car parking space. The property changed hands for a consideration of Rs 10.75 crore, with Rs 64.50 lakh paid as stamp duty.While the sale price is Rs 25 lakh higher than Kher’s purchase price, the appreciation works out to around 2.4% in less than a year. This figure is before factoring in expenses such as stamp duty, registration charges, taxes and other transaction-related costs. Therefore, the difference between the purchase and sale prices should not be treated as Kher’s actual net profit from the deal.The Trade Centre building was developed by Wadhwa Constructions, which sold office spaces in the 10-storey commercial project more than a decade ago. The project received a partial occupation certificate in September 2008 for the third to 10th floors, followed by an occupation certificate in October 2008 for the ground floor and part of the first floor.BKC, among India’s most expensive commercial real estate destinations, has also emerged as a preferred address for celebrities looking to invest in Mumbai property. In 2024, actor R Madhavan bought a residential property in the business district for Rs 17.5 crore. The ready-to-occupy property spans approximately 389 sq m, or 4,182 sq ft, and includes two parking spaces.Known as a major hub for corporate offices, financial institutions and premium commercial developments, BKC continues to attract both businesses and investors. Its connectivity and proximity to major corporate occupiers have helped make the area one of Mumbai’s key commercial destinations, while properties here can also offer potential for rental income and long-term capital appreciation.Get the latest Bollywood & Entertainment News, and more. articles.title: ‘Filmmaking has become like the share market’: Nikkhil Advani on how audiences have changed, why star power no longer guarantees box office success
articles.summary: Director Nikkhil Advani, who has worked with some of Bollywood’s biggest names, including Shah Rukh Khan and Priyanka Chopra Jonas, believes that the .
articles.body: Director Nikkhil Advani, who has worked with some of Bollywood’s biggest names, including Shah Rukh Khan and Priyanka Chopra Jonas, believes that the presence of a major star is no longer enough to guarantee a film’s success. According to the filmmaker, audiences today are more interested in feeling a genuine connection with an actor or a story than simply following star power.In a recent interview with Hindustan Times, Advani also reflected on how audiences have become more independent in their choices and how that shift has changed the way films are marketed and evaluated.Nikkhil Advani on how audiences are changing film marketingAdvani believes today’s audiences, particularly younger viewers, do not want filmmakers or marketing teams to dictate how they should perceive a film. Instead, they want the freedom to discover a project for themselves.“The audiences of today, or the kids of today, I think what they’re shouting loudly is that, ‘You can’t handle us.’ You can’t. So even marketing has changed in the sense, don’t tell us whether it’s good or bad, or it’s mind-blowing or whatever. We will discover. Let us discover this. Tell us the story of how it was made,” he said.Nikkhil Advani questions the growing focus on box office numbersHaving spent more than two decades in the industry, Advani also looked back at why he entered filmmaking in the first place. He recalled wanting to use cinema as a means of artistic expression rather than viewing it primarily through the lens of commercial success.“When I joined filmmaking and knocked on the door of (veteran screenwriter) Saeed Mirza, I wanted to express myself through art and not through box office,” he said.Advani then referred to veteran filmmaker Subhash Ghai’s observation that filmmaking has increasingly begun to resemble the financial markets.“I think what Subhash Ghai said, I was reading somewhere, he said that filmmaking has become like the share market. When did it become that?” he asked.‘It’s supposed to be art’For Advani, the concern is not that cinema needs to be commercially successful, but that commercial considerations may have increasingly begun to influence how artistic work itself is perceived.He cited A R Rahman’s music in ‘Taal’ as an example of how the appreciation of art can sometimes become intertwined with commercial calculations.“When did the appreciation of a great piece of music by A R Rahman in a film called ‘Taal’ become about… how did that change? How did it become a business?” he said.He added, “It’s supposed to be art.”Nikkhil Advani’s work frontOn the professional front, Advani recently directed ‘The Revolutionaries’, a period drama series featuring a young ensemble cast and set against the backdrop of India’s freedom struggle.Get the latest Bollywood & Entertainment News, and more. articles.title: New movies to watch this weekend: See 'Practical Magic 2' in theaters, rent 'One Night Only,' stream 'Supergirl' on HBO Max
articles.summary: Don't sleep on Owen Wilson and Alan Ritchson's crowd-pleasing "Runner," a buddy action-comedy now in theaters.
articles.body:
Welcome to Trust Me, I Watch Everything , a weekly guide to all the new movies out each Friday.

This week's buzziest release is Practical Magic 2 , the nearly 30-years-later sequel to the '90s cult-classic cable TV staple starring Sandra Bullock and Nicole Kidman. But it's a busy week in theaters with plenty of other options, including South Korean blockbuster Hope and the Owen Wilson-Alan Ritchson action-comedy Runner.

If you'd rather stay home, you can now rent or buy One Night Only, the rom-com with a bizarre premise , or check out the latest Jason Statham vehicle, Mutiny.

Want to stick to a streaming service you're likely already paying for? Supergirl lands on HBO Max, and Guy Ritchie's In the Grey starring Jake Gyllenhaal and Henry Cavill hits Starz.

Why I didn't like it: Practical Magic was nobody's idea of a success when it hit theaters way back in 1998 — its box office take was modest at best, and critics were not kind to it. Its cozy fall vibes, (some rather mixed) messaging about sisterhood and female empowerment and fun performances from superstars Sandra Bullock and Nicole Kidman, however, led it to become a seasonal staple on cable television, and it eventually found enough of an audience for a high-profile, nearly-30-years-later sequel to make financial sense in our nostalgia-obsessed world.

I watched the original for the first time ahead of the screening of the new one, and found it to be a tonally confused, badly paced mess, despite committed work from the lead actors, as well as from Dianne Wiest and Stockard Channing as the aunts. The movie is decidedly uninterested in witchcraft, except as a means of advancing its story of love and loss — a potent idea, but one that gets buried beneath various subplots with wildly different tones. Centering this story on two women who are uniquely powerful but must hide it from society lest they be labeled witches is also an interesting concept, though it's muddled by the fact that these women are, canonically, witches.

In Practical Magic 2, based on the fourth book in the popular series by Alice Hoffman , the Owens sisters must confront the dark curse that threatens to unravel their family once and for all. In the original film, the Owens sisters discover a family curse that causes all the men they truly love to die, leading them to adopt two different lifestyles to cope with it. Now, this curse has passed down to Bullock's children, with disastrous consequences.

All the principal actors are back, except for Evan Rachel Wood as one of Bullock's daughters, who was replaced by Joey King , since the characters are meant to be in college. Bullock and Kidman have fantastic chemistry in the movie, and that energy has carried over to the press tour, with viral clips dominating the web in the run-up to the movie's release. Bullock has kept herself so scarce cinematically that seeing her onscreen is always exciting; she feels like one of the few true movie stars we have left who hasn't completely oversaturated the market or overstayed their welcome.

I acknowledge that these movies are not really for me — I want my movies about witches to do more with the dark arts than make margaritas and flicker the lights — and this sequel will likely satisfy fans who are simply eager to spend more time with these characters and their world. I found the movie's use of the legacy-sequel framework uninspiring and was never fully engaged with the story, which I felt hewed too closely to the original, both in content and in the way it's all so loosely connected.

The biggest issue, though, is with the screenplay. The movie is so all over the place that a "villain" is introduced and dealt with within a 10-minute span, then the movie climaxes, ostensibly wrapping everything up, only to go on for another 20 minutes that are absolutely useless and deadly. The plotting on the way there is as perfunctory as it gets, involving a magic book and a trip abroad to find answers dating back to their ancestral home.

Practical Magic 2 is just as dopey as the first movie — arguably more so — but it's certainly going to fare far better than its predecessor at the box office. But hey, I'm all for studios like Warner Bros. mining their back catalogs for unexpectedly viable IP and capitalizing on cult fandom. People who love the first film will likely have a good enough time, and the box office could also use a Sandra Bullock infusion. The best we can hope for is that the next legacy sequel, plucked from onetime obscurity and based on a cable-TV-era cult classic, finds a more compelling reason to exist.

What other critics are saying : Other reviews are similarly brutal. The Telegraph's Tim Robey calls it "the most blatant fan service in years: a blandly watchable but stubbornly inessential sequel to a forgettable 1998 romp." Anna McKibbin at the AV Club writes , "Even if Practical Magic was a beloved part of your childhood, it's hard to see what would excite you about this sequel."

How to watch : Practical Magic 2 is now playing in theaters nationwide .

Why I liked it, with reservations: South Korean director Na Hong-jin is back with his first film since 2016's The Wailing, and it's a propulsive, wacky sci-fi creature feature that delivers blockbuster-sized spectacle in several memorable chase and/or action sequences. It's quite funny too, in ways both big and small.

But Hope is also so deeply weird and strange that much of its crowd-pleasing energy burns off as it goes, culminating in an ending that had the audience I saw it with murmuring "huhs?!" aloud, despite its killer third-act set piece. I also believe that the best sequence happens right up top, when our protagonist keeps almost encountering the monster but only sees the trail of destruction.

The synopsis: In the remote South Korean village of Hope Harbor, a police chief and officer are called to investigate a mysterious creature wreaking havoc on the community. But all is not as it seems, and perceptions can be misleading. What begins as ignorance plants the seed of disaster, which, through human conflict, escalates into a tragedy of cosmic proportions.

The monsters themselves are sure to be a point of controversy, both in their design and in the CGI used to create them. The creatures feel very video-game-y, likely due to the fact that they run faster than any other monster I've ever seen in a movie and are far closer in spirit to unbeatable bosses in a game. There's been lots of talk about how scary it is when Michael Myers and Jason Voorhees walk slowly; we never considered how much more terrifying it would be if they were as fast as jaguars.

Thematically, the movie isn't breaking new ground, as its central idea feels like the flipside of the dynamic explored in Arrival, which concerns miscommunication between different worlds and how that can lead to our destruction. Hope is, ironically, less hopeful ultimately than Arrival, arguing that humans act impulsively without fully understanding the threat they face and are likely doomed as a result.

Hope ekes out a recommendation purely on the strength of its multiple extended set pieces, which are compelling before they start to get a bit repetitive. It may be an unwieldy sight, but it's worth the price of admission.

What other critics are saying : It's getting great marks! Nick Schager at the Daily Beast calls it "an import of larger-than-life imagination and artistry that rarely lets its foot off the gas." The Guardian's Peter Bradshaw writes, "There is some top-quality entertainment value on offer here from a movie which can only intensify the world's K-obsession."

How to watch : Hope is now playing in theaters nationwide .

Why I liked it: A mismatched buddy action-comedy starring Owen Wilson? Welcome back, early 2000s!

In the latest flick from Angel Studios, whose theatrical footprint has really grown this year , a former soldier and his unlikely partner become the targets of a ruthless cartel while racing to complete a critical medical delivery and save the life of a little girl.

To get a bit more specific, Owen Wilson plays a guy transporting an organ on ice with a very specific, fast-approaching expiration date. This makes the organ highly sought after by bad people, as it would fetch a ton of money on the black market … or maybe somebody has another reason for wanting it.

Ritchson plays the extremely reluctant courier hired to transport Wilson, and his dedication to getting the job done at any cost really helps power the movie. The action is exciting and fun, and the banter between Ritchson and Wilson is a hoot and harkens back to a bygone era of Wilson-starring action-comedies. The plot is simply an excuse to showcase chase and action sequences, and the movie capitalizes on every opportunity, using some really clever camerawork.

I found Runner to be about 10,000% better than I expected based solely on its poster and premise. They should teach it in film school to show how even tired, formulaic material can work when it's handled with care and performed well. I was totally in the palm of the movie's hand. It's an unexpectedly crowd-pleasing charmer that I hope finds an audience and becomes a sleeper hit. It's a great time at the movies.

What other critics are saying : They're similarly impressed, relatively speaking. Todd Gilchrist at Variety writes, "This clunky vehicle doesn't transcend its limitations — Wilson and Ritchson's efforts are the duct tape holding it together — but it's much better than anyone could have expected." TheWrap's William Bibbiani calls it "the porridge Goldilocks ate, if Goldilocks loved kicking butt and taking names."

How to watch : Runner is now playing in theaters nationwide .

The Uprising: This perfectly serviceable but rather dull historical action film is overtly political and doesn't have to tie itself in knots to make connections between the 1381 Peasants' Revolt in England and how wealth and power function today. It's not subtle about it; the rebelling commoners are at one point referred to as "deplorables." Andrew Garfield plays the leader of a ferocious rebellion against the tyranny of King Richard II, forming an army of the people to face the king's might in a fight for justice. The most interesting thing about this movie is, unfortunately, extratextual, as the U.S. marketing pivoted late in the game to calling it The Uprising: The Rise of Robin Hood and stressing that the film was "set against the true events of the uprising that helped inspire the legend of Robin Hood," even as the non-U.S. marketing departments insisted that it was not, in fact, about Robin Hood. I can confirm, dear reader, that the movie does, in fact, pivot to a stealth origin story for Robin Hood eventually, much like it unfolded in the press: at the absolute last minute! It's far more compelling as a movie about the Peasants' Revolt than as a Robin Hood picture, and that's without getting into the muddying of timelines for those who care about historical accuracy. Get tickets

The Fix : I'm not sure this war-torn action flick with Zachary Levi and Liam Neeson needed to be two and a half hours, but I'd be lying if I didn't acknowledge that it held my attention throughout. Disillusioned by the end of the war in Afghanistan, a group of disgraced ex-CIA operatives set out for Tehran to take down a life-changing score. Its well-staged battle sequences make the action feel immediate, and the plot's busyness is well handled through taut cross-cutting as it turns into a high-stakes heist flick. It works, and Levi really nails the part. Don't expect to see much Neeson, though — he's barely in it. Get tickets.

Oasis: Don't Look Back in Anger: This hybrid documentary-concert film highlights Oasis's massive 2025 reunion tour, including raw rehearsal footage, backstage access and the first joint interview with Liam and Noel Gallagher in over 15 years. Fans of the band are in for an unexpectedly emotional treat. Get tickets.

Editor's note: My Yahoo colleague Kelsey Weekman reviewed this one.

Why I liked it: One Night Only has one of the most compelling and strange premises I've ever seen in a romantic comedy: What if extramarital sex were outlawed, except for one night a year, during which people completely lose their minds?

Allie (Monica Barbaro) and Owen (Callum Turner) play, respectively, a pharmaceutical jingle singer (a great running bit) and a pizza shop owner, who, for varying reasons, are hunting for a human connection (literally) on the least romantic night of the year. The bizarre rules of the night keep getting in their way, tearing them apart, then bringing them back together.

What I didn't expect was how much I full-body laughed at the gags in the kooky dystopian landscape, which is portrayed as more ridiculous than harrowing. There's a parade of celebrity cameos (King Princess! One of the Haim sisters! Pete Davidson! LeVar Burton!) who shuttle the plot along nicely by weaving in and out of the paths of our protagonists.

In our actual dystopian world, where it's hard to find a funny romance that doesn't feel like streaming algorithm slop, I don't mind a few enemies-to-lovers tropes sprinkled into a genuinely original idea. That said, I recognize a movie with such a banger of a premise is going to fall short of many moviegoers' expectations. Don't go in expecting incisive political commentary, though it's not entirely devoid of that — people speak out against "the mandate," but they give themselves fully to the chaos of the night as well. After all, there are 364 other nights of the year for protest.

Before you go, consider how the fictional ban might be enforced, what the punishment might be, where the loopholes are and why a puritanical society might allow one night of release. Theorizing about the technicalities of the sex Purge might be more fun than the movie itself.

What other critics are saying : I admit I liked it more than most. TheWrap's Matt Goldberg writes that there are "plenty of gags along the way paired with the strong chemistry between leads," adding that it "feels like the kind of movie that shouldn't work, and you're delighted that it does." On the other hand, the New York Times' Natalia Winkelman writes , "With nothing to say about sex or society, the repression plot mostly gets in the way of a movie that would prefer to be a routine romance."

How to watch : One Night Only is now available to rent or buy on Apple TV , Prime Video and other VOD platforms.

Why I found it ... OK: Jason Statham's latest Jason Statham movie delivers exactly what you'd expect from it, and not an ounce more.

After witnessing his billionaire boss's murder and being framed for the crime, Cole Reed (Statham) boards a cargo ship on a one-man crusade to avenge the death, only to discover an international human trafficking conspiracy.

It's about as boilerplate as it gets and plays more like a straight-to-video variant of this type of thing. But it does really come alive in the action scenes, especially the first one, which is highlighted in the trailer above.

Unfortunately, there aren't quite enough of those sequences for this to rank in the top tier of Statham joints. They're selling it as " Die Hard on a boat" as if Steven Seagal didn't already do that way back in 1992.

What other critics are saying : It's an even split! Amy Nicholson at the Los Angeles Times writes, "No one is going to see Mutiny for the plot, some will counter. Fair point. I'll go further and say Mutiny would be improved if it hadn't bothered with a script at all and simply titled the film " Thirty Kills in 95 Minutes ." Ben Lee at the Guardian writes, "The action genre is undoubtedly in need of new tricks, but until they come, films like Mutiny offer a modestly entertaining reminder of what the old dogs can still do."

How to watch : Mutiny is now available to rent or buy on Apple TV , Prime Video and other VOD platforms.

Moana : You'd think a super-expensive "live-action" remake of Moana would nail the basics, like having the titular character sailing on the water. I put "live-action" in quotes because damn near every element onscreen in this latest Disney double-dip cash-grab is still digital and fake, just far uglier and less colorful than it was before . It's a hideously ugly, low-rent production that looks and feels like a cheap theme-park cosplay experience rather than an actual movie. As far as adapting the material goes, it's basically a word-for-word, shot-for-shot copy of the original. When you factor in that it's only been a decade since the original debuted and just a year and a half since the release of its hastily produced animated sequel (really just a few episodes of a planned Disney+ series strung together), it strains credulity even more. Just watch the original animated version on Disney+ instead. Rent or buy.

Why I didn't like it: As a noted hater of James Gunn's Superman but a big fan of the comic book series that this new movie is based on ( Supergirl: Woman of Tomorrow, by writer Tom King and artist Bilquis Evely), I had high hopes for Supergirl. The movie did not meet them.

Milly Alcock of HBO's House of the Dragon stars as Clark Kent's cousin Kara Zor-El, and here's what passes for a plot: When an unexpected and ruthless adversary strikes too close to home, Kara Zor-El, aka Supergirl, reluctantly joins forces with an unlikely companion on an epic, interstellar journey of vengeance and justice.

While the movie technically adapts the comic book's story, it does so in such disastrous ways that they might as well have left the source material alone. In Woman of Tomorrow, you are made to feel how evil marauding space villain Krem is; he comes off quite menacing and scary on the page. In the movie, we know he's bad because he's made up to look like a Mad Max villain, with studs in his face and the like. It's a great look, but that's not characterization, and he has none here. Thus, an A-grade villain becomes a generic, forgettable bad guy.

Even worse, Ruthye, the Supergirl ally who is such a key part in the books, gets sidelined in a way that makes her annoying and useless. Her arc in the comic mirrors Mattie's in Charles Portis's legendary novel True Grit, and even her dialogue throughout the series makes it clear that's what they're going for. The movie abandons all of this to give us … Jason Momoa as Lobo, a fan-favorite bounty hunter character who has no business being in the movie at all, and a fetch-quest plot centered around the poisoning of a CGI dog that was already overutilized in the last movie. The story of Woman of Tomorrow is such a layup, and they give it up for no good reason.

The movie plays like a Star Wars cantina band-scene compilation for a while as Kara and friends traverse the galaxy to track down the antidote to the poison or whatever. It's one Mos Eisley after another! These sequences feature some fun, practical makeup on the monsters and cool-looking sets mixed in with awful-looking digital effects, which only serve to emphasize how muddy and bad the movie looks the rest of the time.

Supergirl, worst of all, shortchanges Kara, who feels like she's second- or third-string in her own movie at times. She doesn't get to do anything "super," really, and is often seen just floating around, which, again, looks terrible because these movies are now all shot in warehouses with backgrounds added in post. It's clear that Momoa's Lobo is shoehorned in because somebody at Warner Bros. was worried that a female-centric superhero movie wouldn't sell enough tickets. You could excise his character from the movie entirely and lose nothing. In fact, it would be better. And I've barely mentioned how incoherent and useless the action sequences are; not a single one makes an impression, unless what they were going for is me squinting to see what the hell is happening.

Supergirl goes in a decidedly different direction from Superman, leaning more into Star Wars territory, which, combined with the reverence the movie shows for its needle drops, makes it feel like another attempt at Guardians of the Galaxy. The Mad Max aesthetic is cool, but those movies work because they have the action and spectacle to back it up. Supergirl does not, nor does it have an actual story to engage with.

The one-two punch of Superman and Supergirl was supposed to usher in an exciting and bold new era at DC, despite industry headwinds suggesting that superhero movies have lost their luster. Instead, all they've done is prove there's not much juice left to squeeze.

What other critics are saying: It was torn apart! Clarisse Loughrey at the Independent writes, "The mandate here appears to be to keep things as distinctly Gunn-esque as possible. In return, Superman's moodier, more cynical relative has been robbed of the chance to speak with her own voice. It's the superhero equivalent of a Vegas impersonator." Robbie Collin at the Telegraph says it's "like watching an endless orangey-gray rehash of scenes from Mad Max and Star Wars . Who is faster than a speeding bullet and can leap tall buildings in a single bound? Supergirl 's novel answer: Who cares?"

How to watch : Supergirl is now streaming on HBO Max .

Why I liked it: The latest caper from Guy Ritchie sports a top-notch cast and a whole bunch of exposition, but if you're a fan of Ritchie's output, it's another well-directed and edited B-picture.

When a ruthless despot steals a billion-dollar fortune, a covert team of elite operatives is sent to take it back, and an impossible heist erupts into a deadly game of strategy, deception and survival.

It's a good, old-fashioned programmer that feels like they made the entire movie out of the pre-heist montage; imagine Ocean's 11 if the entire runtime were devoted to the characters detailing what they're about to do, and then doing it. It's been trimmed of all excess and is a lean, mean, "extended set-up followed by an action set-piece" machine. It's meticulous planning made cinematic through Ritchie's sheer bombast.

I found it a lot of fun, and it's frankly too bad it bombed at the box office, because I would've easily watched one of these every year. Thankfully, Ritchie's output has been staggering lately, and hopefully, this one tanking won't stop him.

What other critics are saying : It's a real mixed bag. Jesse Hassenger at the AV Club dug it, writing, "Anyone who enjoys Ritchie's now-annual adventures can safely surrender to this one." TheWrap's William Bibbiani writes, "It's a one-way ticket to Dullsville. Population: this poor, poor cast."

How to watch : In The Grey is streaming on Starz beginning Saturday, Sept. 12.

Driver's Ed: This throwback charmer, directed by Bobby Farrelly, one-half of the legendary comedic filmmaking duo, plays like an '80s teen comedy à la The Breakfast Club or Ferris Bueller's Day Off, despite a plot straight out of something more early 2000s like Road Trip. (It's decidedly less raunchy, though.) What it lacks in big-swing laughs, it makes up for in earnest observations about a very specific time in life, the transition from high school to college, and the relationships that wind up as unintended casualties of that situation, no matter how strong the bond between the two people involved. The plot involves a group of teens stealing their school's driver's ed car for a road trip to help a high school senior track down his college freshman girlfriend and win her back. The teens learn valuable life lessons along the way, as Molly Shannon, Kumail Nanjiani, and Tim Baltz earn lots of laughs as the adults trying to get them home without involving the authorities. It's nowhere near the level of Farrelly material, but it's warm, honest and funny enough to recommend because it treats its characters like real people rather than archetypes . Now streaming on Paramount+ .

That's all for this week! We'll see you next Friday.

articles.title: Pete Davidson says becoming a dad changed how he views father's death on 9/11
articles.summary: Pete Davidson revealed this 9/11 anniversary is "extra tough" now that he's the same age his firefighter dad was when he died at the World Trade Center.
articles.body: Pete Davidson is now the same age — 33 — that his firefighter dad was when he died on 9/11. "I thought, ‘Oh, he was an old guy. He’s 33,’" Davidson told the New York Post in a recent interview. "But now I’m there, and I have a kid, and that would be like my kid not having her dad." To mark 25 years since the tragedy, Davidson is participating in a comedy benefit at Madison Square Garden with Jon Stewart. FOX NEWS MEDIA ANNOUNCES EXTENSIVE 9/11 ANNIVERSARY COVERAGE FROM GROUND ZERO, PENTAGON AND SHANKSVILLE "So, this year is extra tough, but also extra beautiful because I get to spend the day with Scottie," he said of his daughter who was born last December and is named after his late father. "It’ll be very healing and special." Davidson shares Scottie with ex-girlfriend Elsie Hewitt. "It was really cool that Elsie also wanted to name her Scottie," he told the Post. "My dad’s name was Scott, but his nickname was Scotty. When she arrived, we both looked at her and were like, ‘She looks like a Scottie.’ It’s nice to keep that name alive." The "Saturday Night Live" alum is also looking forward to using the comedy benefit as a way of "reclaim[ing]" the day and just having "fun." PETE DAVIDSON SAYS YOUNG PEOPLE 'DON'T HAVE A SHOT' AT FINDING LOVE "And not be in the middle of 12 documentaries that are so sad and rehash it," he added. Davidson explained on Theo Von’s podcast last year that his dad's crew was the first truck over the bridge to the World Trade Center. FRANK SILLER: 'I LOVE YOU, BROTHER' -- THE 9/11 LOSS THAT INSPIRED A MISSION OF SERVICE "So they were the first truck over there and pretty much the whole house died, which is sad, but at least he died with his pals." Davidson called his dad "f---ing hilarious." "My memories are few and far between because I was 7, but I just remember laughing a lot, him being pretty jacked and smoking a lot of cigarettes, and driving a Subaru Impreza. That’s all I remember." He said he also remembers his dad always had a big smile on his face, and old friends who tell Davidson stories about him also light up when they talk about him. 9/11 IS BECOMING HISTORY. MY GENERATION MUST MAKE SURE AMERICA NEVER FORGETS "I was really young, so I didn’t know what the f--- happened, so it hit me later. Like when I was in college, I was like, ‘Oh, I’m pretty angry about this," he revealed. "It’s actually super f---ed up, but I have his badge, like his chain and they, and that’s how they --- you know, cause everybody was pretty burnt up, so that’s how they knew it was him. And I have it, and I just keep it in a safe because, like with my luck, I’ll lose that s---." FORMER 'SATURDAY NIGHT LIVE' STAR PETE DAVIDSON CHECKS INTO WELLNESS CENTER FOR MENTAL HEALTH: REPORT He said he also has his dad’s jacket, which he used to have on display in his home but decided to take down because it could be a depressing reminder all the time. Davidson’s mom has pictures of his dad everywhere in her home. He said, "But it’s kind of haunting where you’re just like I would like the option, like if I want to go down memory lane I can, but like just like to have your dad staring at you every day…" AS AMERICAN PRIDE HITS A 25-YEAR LOW, A NEW 9/11 EDUCATION PLATFORM URGES THE NATION TO NEVER FORGET Davidson told the Post that he’s not sure how he’ll tell his daughter about how her grandfather died. "Luckily, I have some time," he said. "Honestly, this year is way harder than it’s been in a really long time because I have Scottie, and now I’m the age that my dad was when he died," he admitted. "So I’m just kind of like, ‘Holy s--t.’" In 2023, Davison told the "Real Ones" podcast that his father told him he would pick him up from school on 9/11, but he was picked up by his mother, who didn’t tell him anything for three days. GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE He said his mom was 30 at the time. "I wouldn’t know what the f--- to do and that’s why, when I get older, I’m like, ‘Man, my mom was awesome. I was like f---, she really loves me, like d--n, like f---, that was like rough." "She kept telling me ‘Dad’s at work, coming home,’ whatever. I had no idea." His mom told him he was grounded and not allowed to watch TV, but he said he turned it on one night, "and I just saw my dad on TV … And they’re like ‘these are all the firemen that are like dead and all that s---." "And then sometimes I know the youth on the internet uses 9/11 memes as jokes. Someone will be like, ‘This song’s fire,’ and then they’ll post the towers … and we’re the ones that have to see that s--- all the time," he said. articles.title: India Martínez anuncia que está embarazada de siete meses: "Empieza el proyecto más bonito de nuestras vidas"
articles.standfirst: La cantante dará a luz a su primer hijo en apenas dos meses
articles.summary: La cantante dará a luz a su primer hijo
articles.body: India Martínez ha anunciado que está embarazada de su primer hijo junto a su pareja, Ismael Vázquez. La cantante cordobesa de 40 años ha sorprendido a sus seguidores en Instagram al revelar que se encuentra en el séptimo mes de gestación, por lo que dará a luz en apenas dos meses. "Hace siete meses empezó el proyecto más bonito de nuestras vidas. Os queremos compartir esta noticia con toda nuestra ilusión y nuestro amor", ha escrito la artista junto a dos imágenes. Es en la primera donde la pareja aparece dándose un beso, acompañados de varias ecografías previas del bebé. En la siguiente, India posa sola luciendo su tripa. India Martínez e Ismael Vázquez llevan 15 años juntos. Su relación comenzó en el año 2011, cuando se conocieron en el gimnasio propiedad de Ismael, donde él trabajaba como instructor y especialista de cine. Sin embargo, la historia de cómo se conocieron tiene una anécdota muy divertida, ya que su primer encuentro comenzó con un pequeño desencuentro. Cuando la cantante cordobesa acudió a apuntarse a las instalaciones, Ismael, que era el dueño del gimnasio y trabajaba allí como instructor, no la dejó entrar en un primer momento. El motivo fue que India intentaba colar a dos amigos suyos de forma un tanto disimulada. En ese instante, Ismael no tenía ni idea de quién era ella y la frenó en seco diciéndole de forma directa: "Perdona, ¿dónde vas?". A pesar de ese tenso, pero cómico, inicio, India se inscribió en el centro y comenzó a entrenar bajo su supervisión. Dicho esto, cabe destacar que este anuncio da respuesta al misterioso retiro temporal de los escenarios que la intérprete de ‘Nuestro mundo’ comunicó a sus fans el pasado mes de diciembre.

articles.title: La desgarradora confesión de Emma Heming sobre Bruce Willis: "Estamos constantemente en un estado de duelo"
articles.standfirst: La mujer del actor explica cómo la demencia frontotemporal está afectando a toda la familia y revela cómo sus hijas afrontan el deterioro de su padre
articles.summary: La mujer del actor explica cómo la demencia frontotemporal está afectando a toda la familia y revela cómo sus hijas afrontan el deterioro de su padre
articles.body: Emma Heming Willis ha vuelto a romper su silencio sobre uno de los momentos más difíciles de su vida junto a Bruce Willis. La enfermedad del actor continúa avanzando y su mujer ha reconocido que convivir con la demencia frontotemporal supone para toda la familia un proceso marcado por el dolor, pero también por el amor y la unión. En una entrevista con Hello!, Emma Heming ha puesto palabras a una sensación especialmente difícil de explicar: el duelo por una persona que sigue estando presente. "Estamos constantemente en un estado de duelo", ha confesado al hablar de cómo afrontan ella y las hijas del actor el avance de la enfermedad. La mujer del protagonista de 'La jungla de cristal' ha descrito la situación como "extremadamente difícil y dolorosa", aunque ha querido dejar claro que Bruce continúa muy presente en la vida de su familia. "Todos queremos que nuestros seres queridos estén sanos, llenos de vida y sean quienes siempre fueron. Pero la demencia frontotemporal es una enfermedad devastadora que te va arrebatando cosas muy lentamente", ha explicado. Uno de los testimonios más emotivos de la entrevista tiene que ver con las hijas del intérprete y con la manera en la que están viviendo el deterioro de su padre. Emma Heming asegura que, pese a lo doloroso de la situación, las niñas están siendo testigos de una auténtica lección de amor familiar. "Lo que nuestras hijas viven y presencian en casa cada día es una lección magistral de amor puro", ha afirmado. Las pequeñas ven cómo la familia se mantiene al lado de Bruce Willis y cómo amigos y allegados han creado un "círculo protector" a su alrededor. "Ven cuánto apoyamos a su padre, cuánto lo amamos y cómo lo acompañamos en las buenas y en las malas", ha señalado Emma Heming, que considera que esta experiencia les está enseñando "el verdadero significado de la lealtad, la devoción y el amor incondicional". Emma Heming también ha querido desmontar una de las principales confusiones que existen alrededor de la enfermedad de Bruce Willis. El actor no tiene alzhéimer, sino demencia frontotemporal, una enfermedad que afecta a otras áreas del cerebro y que puede provocar alteraciones en el comportamiento, la personalidad y el lenguaje, entre otros síntomas. De hecho, asegura que una de las preguntas que más recibe cuando habla de su marido es si todavía la recuerda. "Mi respuesta siempre es un rotundo sí", ha afirmado. La empresaria considera que esta pregunta refleja hasta qué punto persisten algunos mitos sobre la demencia frontotemporal. Por ello, ha querido insistir en que el diagnóstico de Bruce Willis no significa que todos los momentos junto a él estén marcados por la tristeza. A pesar de la dureza del proceso, Emma Heming ha querido compartir también un mensaje de esperanza. La esposa del actor considera que existe una visión demasiado negativa de la demencia como una enfermedad que convierte cada instante en sufrimiento. "La idea de que la demencia es una miseria implacable y absoluta cada minuto del día es un mito absoluto", ha asegurado. Según explica Emma Heming, la familia todavía disfruta de momentos cotidianos de felicidad y humor. "Tenemos muchísimos momentos cotidianos que todavía nos resultan graciosos y, afortunadamente, seguimos riendo", ha confesado. Sus palabras reflejan así una realidad compleja: el avance de una enfermedad devastadora convive con momentos de amor, complicidad y normalidad. Una forma de afrontar el día a día que, para Emma Heming, pasa por acompañar a Bruce Willis en cada etapa y encontrar pequeños espacios de felicidad incluso en medio de uno de los momentos más difíciles que ha vivido la familia.

articles.title: New York City’s last pickpocket doesn’t need a smartphone
articles.summary: TIFF 2026 includes anticipated films like The Only Living Pickpocket in New York, All of a Sudden, and the Netflix series Below.
articles.body: Hello once again from Toronto, where for a week every year I watch far too many movies and tell you all about them. The festival, better known as TIFF, is always a great preview of the months ahead in film, with a nice mix of mainstream fare, awards contenders, indie surprises, and genre flicks destined to be cult classics. The streamers also love to make their presence felt here, previewing some of their most anticipated projects. Last year, for instance, Netflix showed off both Guillermo del Toro’s long-awaited Frankenstein as well as the third Knives Out movie, and I was also able to watch everything from the terrifying video game adaptation Exit 8 to Park-Chan wook’s dark satire No Other Choice. This year looks similarly promising. There are new films from directors like Takashi Miike, Ryûsuke Hamaguchi, and Werner Herzog, and very intriguing features including a four-hour-long documentary on Elon Musk. There are also previews of a surprising number of Halloween-adjacent streaming series in the form of Netflix’s Below, Peacock’s Crystal Lake, and Amazon’s Carrie. I’m aiming to see just shy of 30 films and series over the next week or so, and, just like last year, I’ll be writing daily dispatches covering every single thing I see with a brief review. And things have gotten off to a very interesting start. On my first day I watched four movies and the premiere of a streaming series, highlighted by John Turturro’s wonderful turn as a technophobic petty thief in The Only Living Pickpocket in New York. I also saw one of the most Canadian things I’ve ever watched and a three-hour drama that somehow doesn’t feel overlong. Here, in no particular order, is what I’ve seen so far. [Media: The Only Living Pickpocket in New York In theaters on October 30th Imagine if Uncut Gems was a little less stressful, but much more heart-wrenching. Harry (Turturro) is an aging pickpocket, one who sticks to what he knows while the world advances around him. He doesn’t understand smartphones, has no idea what USB means, and laments that no one carries cash anymore. But he’s still able to make a dishonest living and take care of his sick wife. Then one day he accidentally steals a crypto gizmo from the wrong guy, and is pulled into a tense thriller that puts everyone around him at risk. The film is a beautiful love letter to the city of New York, with lots of shots of busy streets and packed subways, but it’s mostly an incredible showcase for Turturro. He plays a genuinely bad guy, but you can’t help but love him in spite of it; at one point he literally steals candy from a child, and it made me smile. The final moments of the film are just about perfect. [Media: All of a Sudden In theaters on November 25th A story about conversation and connection, and one that — despite being over three hours long — absolutely breezes by, much like a great evening out where you suddenly realize it’s 2AM. Split between France and Japan, and helmed by Drive My Car director Ryusuke Hamaguchi, All of a Sudden comes to life after a chance meeting between Marie-Lou (Virginie Efira), the workaholic director of a nursing home, and Mari (Tao Okamoto), a playwright who is coping with a terminal cancer diagnosis. The two connect instantly and spend an entire night talking about everything from the ruinous impact of capitalism to the practical aspects of caring for elderly patients. It all feels natural and heartfelt, though, and at its core, All of a Sudden is a movie about what it means to be human: how we want to spend our time, and how we treat those around us, particularly those who are different or difficult. It sounds cliché, but it left me feeling both hopeful and terrified for the future. The film is also downright gorgeous, and there’s a good chance you’ll immediately start pricing tickets to Paris or Kyoto after you step out of the theater. [Media: Below Streaming on Netflix on October 8th Below is the rare story set in Newfoundland, on the east coast of Canada. It’s a compelling creature feature, a thriller where a mysterious monster is slowly terrorizing a remote fishing village that has been decimated by dwindling fish stocks. Josh Hartnett stars as a father of three who is just trying to survive, when strange chunks of ice start appearing in the harbor, portending something real bad. I watched the first two (of six) episodes, and even though it’s pretty clear what is going on, the show does a remarkable job of building up the mood and suspense, which makes the horrific reveals hit harder. Below is also surprisingly authentic and funny; anyone who has been to the East Coast will feel right at home when they see a bucket of salt beef or the dreaded screech. [Media: Rogue Trooper No theatrical date yet An animated satirical sci-fi movie based on the comic of the same name, Duncan Jones’ Rogue Trooper is set on a toxic planet that is home to a never-ending war that is a lucrative venture back on Earth. It follows a squad of genetically engineered supersoldiers who find themselves stranded in enemy territory, and their numbers steadily dwindle over the course of the film. Unfortunately, despite some occasionally beautiful sci-fi imagery that imbues a real sense of scale, Rogue Trooper mostly falls flat, with a drab story, forgettable characters, and action that lacks any real weight. Even worse, despite boasting a cast including Jemaine Clement, Matthew Berry, and Philomena Cunk herself, Diane Morgan, it’s also not funny at all. [Image: How We Stand No theatrical date yet After moving to Los Angeles as part of the Indian Relocation Act in the 1950s, three sisters find themselves separated from each other after their mother is killed. The story then jumps forward a few decades, when each sister is living a very different life; one is trying to make it as an actress despite being typecast, one is a doctor after being adopted by a white family, and the youngest is struggling after passing through dozens of foster families. How We Stand explores the real impact of some truly horrific policies and programs, and the trio of actors at its core — Amber Midthunder, Alyssa Wapanatâhk, and Isabel DeRoy-Olson — are all excellent. But the film is saddled with writing that can feel too on the nose, and its magical realism elements feel underutilized until the very end.

articles.title: Rob Riggle recalls 'apocalyptic' scene at Ground Zero while searching for survivors after 9/11
articles.summary: Rob Riggle recalls the "apocalyptic" scene at Ground Zero as part of the bucket brigade, describing burned fire trucks and skyscrapers gutted by debris.
articles.body: Rob Riggle is looking back at 9/11 and the "apocalyptic" scene he witnessed while assisting at Ground Zero. During a recent interview with Fox News Digital, the actor and retired U.S. Marine officer recalled the scene at Ground Zero following the terror attacks on the World Trade Center in New York, calling it a "surreal" thing to process. "It was so unreal that it was surreal," he said. "I was looking at skyscrapers that had the front of the building clawed out from the falling of the towers. They had gouged out other buildings. They had knocked other buildings over. They had weakened buildings to such a state that they would collapse." He remembered seeing the Brooks Brothers store across the street from the towers, saying "it looked like Godzilla had scratched out the front" of the building, as it "was all gutted out from where falling debris had smashed into" it. SALVATION ARMY RESPONDER OPENS UP ON 9/11 CANCER BATTLE, PHONE CALL THAT CHANGED HIS LIFE "Then you had burned-out fire trucks and police cars and there were pictures and paper debris, and it was just, it was surreal," he explained. "It was surreal to see that much of Manhattan laying in some sort of apocalyptic ruin. It was shocking, and it was hard to process for sure." Riggle was on site working as a member of the U.S. Marine Corps Reserve based in Manhattan. He was among firefighters, police officers, military personnel, construction workers and volunteers who lined up and cleared debris by hand in buckets. They avoided using machinery to remove the rubble, in order to avoid hurting potential survivors trapped underneath. "Everybody was spread out, so when we stopped, you didn't always know necessarily what was going on," he shared. "Were we dropping a listening device into the rubble? Did they find someone? Did they find someone alive or did they find remains? You just never really knew what it was, and so when they blew the whistle to stop moving and stop working, you would pray, you would just put your head down, and you would hope that it was somebody who was still alive." He added that if they discovered remains, he and the others would say a prayer for them and "that their family would get closure," in addition to praying for themselves, so that they would "have strength to keep going, and hopefully find someone soon." One thing that stood out to Riggle about the days following the terror attacks was the unity among all Americans, saying it was "a unification that I hadn't seen maybe in my entire life." He went on to explain that it didn't matter to anyone what anyone's political beliefs were, and that "it didn't feel like there was anything separating us." "I remember, nobody asked any questions, no one looked at each other and judged down at Ground Zero. Everybody worked. And we were unified in trying to figure out what happened and then figuring out a way to help." LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? Riggle explained that, for many, 9/11 was "very sobering," because it came with the realization that, "there's people out there that are willing to commit evil acts and do harmful things," but what he likes to focus on is that "for every one terrorist, there were literally thousands of people out there trying to do the right thing." For him, when people say "never forget", it means remembering the innocent lives that were lost, and that "there are more good people than bad people." articles.title: R Madhavan’s son Vedaant talks about Asian Games 2026 training, earlier the ‘Dhurandhar’ actor revealed his 4am discipline: ‘Focusing on weight training for 200m freestyle’
articles.summary: R Madhavan’s son Vedaant is gearing up for one of the biggest challenges of his swimming career. The 21-year-old is set to lead India’s 12-member swim.
articles.body: R Madhavan’s son Vedaant is gearing up for one of the biggest challenges of his swimming career. The 21-year-old is set to lead India’s 12-member swimming contingent at the 2026 Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan, where he will compete in the 200m freestyle. A long-distance specialist, Vedaant is stepping outside his comfort zone for the event and has significantly altered his training programme to prepare for the competition.Vedaant said having the right mindset is crucial. “I feel like if you want to succeed in life, you have to be kind of egotistical, where in your mind it’s already fixed, and you know that you’re going to win no matter what," he said in an interview with PTI.Vedaant has primarily competed as a long-distance swimmer but will take on the 200m freestyle at the Asian Games. The change has required him to focus more heavily on strength and conditioning as he prepares for the shorter-distance event as well as the relay.“I’ve actually been training differently for the past few months. As you may know, I’m a long-distance specialist, but I’ll be swimming the 200m freestyle at the Asian Games, which is outside my comfort zone,” he said.He added that his training in recent months has focused extensively on weight training, strengthening his legs and improving his kick and ankle flexibility.“The past few months, I’ve been really focusing on weight training and getting my strength so I can prepare for the relay and the 200m freestyle. So, I’ve taken a whole new approach. One of my weakest points was my legs and my kick, so I’ve been really honing in and working on my kick, my legs, and my ankle flexibility so they can improve. Overall, my stroke is looking a lot better and faster.”Vedaant’s sporting journey has unfolded alongside a parenting philosophy that Madhavan has spoken about at length over the years. During a conversation at an event at the Indian School of Business, the actor admitted that fatherhood itself had been a learning process for him and explained the qualities he believed parents should encourage in their children.“I haven’t completely become successful as a father yet. It’s a work in progress, but I can share the benefit of my experience with you. I have realised that children nowadays are far wiser than we give them credit for. I have also realised that the tools that have worked in my favour to achieve what I have managed to achieve so far can be summed up in one word: grit.”For Madhavan, grit meant combining discipline with ambition. He said one of his priorities as a father was to ensure that Vedaant understood the importance of following a routine.“When I say grit, I mean a combination of discipline and ambition. I wanted to make sure that Vedaant had the ability to follow a routine. If that routine involved getting up early in the morning, then 90 per cent of my problem as a father was solved. If you are someone who is willing to get up early in the morning, you can accomplish a lot.”Swimming eventually became an important part of that routine. Madhavan recalled how Vedaant’s training schedule meant waking up at 4 am, something that also naturally imposed discipline on his teenage years.“He got into swimming, and because he got into swimming, he had to get up at 4 in the morning to train. The best part about getting up at 4 in the morning is that, even as a teenager, he has to sleep by 8 o’clock at night. The problem starts only after 9 o’clock, so I only have to keep an eye on him after 9,” the actor joked.At the same time, Madhavan stressed that parents should know when to step back. Rather than deciding their children’s future for them, he believes they should give them the freedom to discover what genuinely interests them.“The second thing is, you have to let them be. Their exposure to today’s world is far greater than ours. So, if they are able to follow a routine and a process that involves doing something over and over again because they genuinely like it, without you having to force them, then you can be sure that they are well on their way to achieving something.”Madhavan also pointed out that the changing nature of careers makes it difficult for parents to map out a single professional path for their children.“Because in today’s fast-changing world, you can’t really micro-direct them towards a profession, unlike what our fathers used to do. They are unlikely to stick to one profession for their entire lifetime, unlike a lot of people from our generation.”He went on to argue that exposure to different experiences and the ability to remain disciplined could be more valuable than pushing children towards early specialisation.“The vastness of experiences is far more important than specialisation today. So I say, just let them be. Just make sure that they have the discipline to do something over and over again for multiple years while they are with you. Then you can be rest assured that they will have the ability to apply themselves to whatever their interests may be.”According to Madhavan, developing expertise and learning to excel at something can also give children the confidence to apply themselves in other areas.“For them to peak at a much earlier stage today is far more important and relevant.
